rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human life appears to be a succession of confinements and hardships, but reflection reveals that these are divine mercy, so complaint gives way to gratitude.
rows.anchor: لكن حقيقته محض الكرم والرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge and love of God remain in the heart after worldly attachments leave it; they send streams of reflection, listening, and praise through the faculties.
rows.anchor: لما بقيت المعرفة والمحبة في أرض القلب انفجر من هذا الينبوع أنهار وجداول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart becomes a garden for God, so God rewards the servant's limited offering with an everlasting garden from His own abundance.
rows.anchor: جعلت قلبك كالجنة لي وأجريت فيه تلك الأنهار دائمة مخلدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The permanence of the gift compensates for the servant's partial contribution; God gives part of His kingdom eternally and is more generous than the servant.
rows.anchor: وأنا أولى منه بالكرم والجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reward means both a full recompense without deficiency and a sufficiency that leaves no desire unmet, as promised in the verse about desired things in Paradise.
rows.anchor: أنه يعطيه الجزاء الوافر من غير نقص

rows.speaker: أهل السنة
rows.claim: The Sunnis say calling Paradise a reward denotes a conditional recompense in ordinary language, not an intrinsic entitlement against God.
rows.anchor: فهذا شرط وجزاء بحسب اللغة وبحسب الوضع لا بحسب الاستحقاق الذاتي

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites read the gardens as granted through prior grace: creation, capacity, reason, removal of excuses, and divine aid made attainment possible.
rows.anchor: إن كلمة من لابتداء الغاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's past gift of creation lets people benefit from His resources; the author illustrates this with a wealthy owner providing dependents and cites the report that creatures are God's dependents.
rows.anchor: فهو سبحانه اشترى من دار العدم هذا الخلق لينتفعوا بملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: During earthly obligation, beginning an act creates a reason to complete it; the Merciful is even more entitled to complete His benefaction.
rows.anchor: وأما اليومي فالنعمان يوجب الإتمام بعد الشروع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the future, God's own promise and declaration make Him bound by His word, so He fulfills the promised reward.
rows.anchor: وأما الغد فأنا مديونهم بحكم الوعد والإخبار فكيف لا أفي بذلك

rows.speaker: بعض الفقهاء
rows.claim: Some jurists distinguish phrases: having nothing owed concerns debts, having nothing held with someone concerns deposits, and having nothing before someone covers both.
rows.anchor: فهذا يختص بالديون وله أن يدعي الوديعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase with God suggests a deposited asset held in trust, which is nobler than a debt; although deposits can perish, that possibility is impossible with God.
rows.anchor: يفيد أنه كالمال المعين الحاضر العتيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As bodily life faces worldly turmoil, a person can entrust faith to God, who records it and delivers it when most needed at the resurrection.
rows.anchor: فضع وديعة أمانتك عندي فإني أكتب لك به كتابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase at their Lord recalls God's original care: He created people from nonexistence and gave them life, reason, and power, so He will not lose what they entrust to Him.
rows.anchor: أنا الذي ربيتك أولا حين كنت معدوما صفر اليد من الوجود والحياة والعقل والقدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical view matches each person to one garden; an example about two people entering two houses illustrates distributing paired items one by one.
rows.anchor: وهو يقتضي مقابلة الفرد بالفرد

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abu Yusuf holds that the plural wording requires each person to own the gardens together, and that entering both houses is required in the illustrative oath.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي يوسف لم يحنث حتى يدخلا الدارين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the one-garden view, each garden is at least ten times the world; another possibility is several gardens per person, supported by the two pairs promised in the other passage.
rows.anchor: لكن أدنى تلك الجنات مثل الدنيا بما فيها عشر مرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author gives a devotional explanation for four gardens: fear of God produces tears from four eyelids, earning two gardens for each pair of eyes.
rows.anchor: لسكبه البكاء من أربعة أجفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear must persist before action as fear of failure and after action as fear of falling short; the verse's closing phrase points to continuing reverence.
rows.anchor: أما قبل العمل فالحاصل خوف الاختلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAdn means settled residence, supported by verses saying Paradise's people will not leave or be expelled and will seek no change of abode.
rows.anchor: عدن } يفيد الإقامة : { لا يخرجون منها }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report places the Gardens of Eden in the center of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وروى أن جنات عدن وسط الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation derives ʿAdn from a mineral deposit: Paradise is the source of bliss, security, and safety.
rows.anchor: وقيل : عدن من المعدن أي هي معدن النعيم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: If Paradise's name is linked to jinn, the comparison suggests that it conveys a person's desires with extraordinary speed, like jinn crossing the world in an hour.
rows.anchor: فإن كانت من الجن فهم المخصوصون بسرعة الحركة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: If the name is linked to madness, Paradise is so astonishing that a rational person seeing it would nearly lose his mind, were God not to steady him.
rows.anchor: وإما من الجنون فهو أن الجنة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: If the name is linked to a protective garden, Paradise shields people from the Fire.
rows.anchor: وإما من الجنة فلأنها جنة واقية تقيك من النار

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: If its name is linked to an embryo, the people of Paradise are so sheltered and comfortable that they resemble an embryo untouched by heat or cold.
rows.anchor: من الجنين ، فلأن المكلف يكون في الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Running water is more delicate than still water and even viewing it brightens sight; the image also matches worship that continues through life and reward that flows forever.
rows.anchor: أن الماء الجاري ألطف من الراكد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase from beneath prevents annoyance: flowing water removes one garden defect, while its lower course prevents flooding and excess.
rows.anchor: وإما بسبب الغرق والكثرة ، فذكر من تحتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in the rivers points to the rivers named in the Quran: water, milk, honey, and wine.
rows.anchor: الألف واللام في الأنهار للتعريف فتكون منصرفة إلى الأنهار المذكورة في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A river is a broad, bright expanse, not a small channel; the author supports the distinction by setting rivers beside the sea.
rows.anchor: الساقية نهرا ، بل العظيم هو الذي يسمى نهرا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that everlasting life in Paradise is better than Paradise, and God's pleasure is better than Paradise.
rows.anchor: وروى أنه عليه السلام قال : ( إن الخلود في الجنة خير من الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names Garden of Eden, Garden of Bliss, and Abode of Peace correspond to the three elements of faith: belief, speech, and action.
rows.anchor: ركبت إيمانك من أمور ثلاثة اعتقاد وقول وعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bodily garden is the body's Paradise, while God's approval is the soul's garden; the verse moves from bodily origin toward the soul's spiritual end.
rows.anchor: فجنة الجسد هي الجنة الموصوفة وجنة الروح هي رضا الرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's approval comes before theirs because the eternal affects what is originated, whereas the originated cannot affect the eternal.
rows.anchor: الأزلي هو المؤثر في المحدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Allah conveys majesty and all attributes more fully than Lord; complete service is fitting in such a presence, so the wording ennobles the servant's action.
rows.anchor: لأن أشد الأسماء هيبة وجلالة لفظ الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpret God being pleased with them as His being pleased with their deeds.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم : معناه رضي أعمالهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others distinguish approval of a person from approval of an act and take the phrase to mean that God praises and honors them; the author calls this the nearer interpretation.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الأقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their being pleased with God means being content with the bliss and reward He gives them.
rows.anchor: فالمراد أنه رضوا بما جازاهم من النعيم والثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear in obedience is a good spiritual state, and reverent awe may be stronger than fear because it is paired with the angels' intense apprehension.
rows.anchor: والكلام في الخوف والخشية مشهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combining the verse that says only scholars fear God with this promise of Paradise yields the conclusion that Paradise belongs to people of knowledge.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية إذا ضم إليها آية أخرى صار المجموع دليلا على فضل العلم والعلماء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some infer that a person can never become certain of Paradise, but the author rejects this because prophets knew their destination and still feared God greatly.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم : هذه الآية تدل على أن المرء لا ينتهي إلى حد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets can know they are people of Paradise while remaining among God's most fearful servants.
rows.anchor: لأن الأنبياء عليهم السلام قد علموا أنهم من أهل الجنة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet says that the person who knows God best fears Him most, and that he himself fears God most.
rows.anchor: قال عليه الصلاة والسلام : ( أعرفكم بالله أخوفكم من الله ، وأنا أخوفكم منه )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One coherence reading answers when the promised reward arrives: at the earthquake, when all fear but believers receive their reward safely.
rows.anchor: ومتى يكون ذلك يا رب فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another coherence reading extends the previous surah's warning to disbelievers, then turns to both groups and their smallest good or evil deeds.
rows.anchor: أراد أن يزيد في وعيد الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because people asked when the Hour would come, the opening gives its signs rather than assigning a time; alternatively it answers when the earth will testify despite now being inanimate.
rows.anchor: لا سبيل إلى تعيينه بحسب وقته ولكني أعينه بحسب علاماته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the usual distinction, in marks a possible condition, while when marks an event certain to occur; the quake is certain.
rows.anchor: { وإذا } في المقطوع به

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra distinguishes the kasra form as the verbal noun and the fatha form as the event's name; both readings occur, as with waswas.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : الزلزال بالكسر المصدر والزلزال بالفتح الاسم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say the earth itself moves and convulses, rather than being passively moved; its agency across the surah intensifies the terror and admonishes people to wake from heedlessness.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم : ليس المراد من زلزلت حركت ، بل المراد : تحركت واضطربت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root zalla denotes ordinary movement, while the reduplicated form indicates repeated, intense movement; the Hour's quake is called tremendous.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن زل للحركة المعتادة ، وزلزل للحركة الشديدة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the quake as the first blast, followed by another shaking that raises the dead as the earth's burdens.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد : المراد من الزلزلة المذكورة في هذه الآية النفخة الأولى

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others identify it as the second quake because the earth's release of its burdens is one of that quake's consequences.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : هذه الزلزلة هي الثانية بدليل أنه تعالى جعل من لوازمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possessive in its quake can mean the degree appropriate to the earth, as one speaks of giving a pious person fitting honor or a wicked person fitting disgrace.
rows.anchor: القدر اللائق بها في الحكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, its quake means the complete measure the earth can bear: everything possible of shaking occurs.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المعنى زلزالها كله وجميع ما هو ممكن منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading takes it as the quake promised or written for the earth, treating it as living; a report attributes its shaking to Israfil's tremendous sound.
rows.anchor: الثالث : { زلزالها } الموعود أو المكتوب عليها إذا قدرت تقدير الحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word burdens can mean possessions; Abu ʿUbayda and al-Akhfash say a buried dead person weighs on the earth, while above-ground people weigh upon it, hence humans and jinn are the two burdens.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة والأخفش : إذا كان الميت في بطن الأرض فهو ثقل لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first-quake view, the earth expels its buried treasures, yet no one will care for the gold; alternatively the treasure's display rebukes people who ruined life and faith for it.
rows.anchor: يعني الكنوز فيمتلىء ظهر الأرض ذهبا ولا أحد يلتفت إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the second-quake view, the earth brings the dead out alive, like a mother delivering a living child.
rows.anchor: تخرج الأثقال يعني الموتى أحياء كالأم تلده حيا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view says the earth first ejects the dead as dead, just as they were buried, and God then revives them.
rows.anchor: كما دفن ثم يحييه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second meaning of burdens is the earth's secrets, exposed on that day so it can testify for or against people.
rows.anchor: أثقالها : أسرارها فيومئذ تكشف الأسرار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth first holds people in its protective embrace, as another verse says, then reverses course and casts them out, like the coming scenes of terror and flight.
rows.anchor: ثم صارت بحال ترميك وهو تقرير لقوله :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question asks why the earth shakes so violently and ejects what it contains, whether treasures at the first blast or the dead at the second.
rows.anchor: مالها تزلزل هذه الزلزلة الشديدة ولفظت ما في بطنها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the speaker to be a disbeliever, echoing the question about who raised people from their resting place; believers instead affirm God's promise and the truth of the messengers.
rows.anchor: قيل : هذا قول الكافر وهو كما يقولون : { ياويلنا من بعثنا من مرقدنا }

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the question is common to disbelievers and sinners; it is an exclamation of astonishment, not a request for information, from humanity's usual heedlessness.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال : الحسن إنه للكافر والفاجر معا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indirect wording turns the reproach inward: the self blames its sins for the earth's state; disbelievers ask what is happening while believers praise God for removing grief.
rows.anchor: يا نفس أنت السبب فيه فإنه لولا معاصيك لما صارت الأرض كذلك

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud reads the verb as the earth telling its reports.
rows.anchor: أن ابن مسعود قرأ : { تحدث أخبارها }

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr reads the verb as the earth informing people of its reports.
rows.anchor: وسعيد بن جبير تنبيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb's first object is omitted; its second is its reports. Suppressing the people who receive the news keeps attention on the earth's telling and magnifies it.
rows.anchor: قد حذف أولهما والثاني أخبارها وأصله تحدث الخلق أخبارها

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says the quake makes everyone understand the end of worldly life and the arrival of the afterlife, like a house that tells us it was once inhabited.
rows.anchor: وهو قول أبي مسلم يومئذ يتبين لكل أحد جزاء عمله

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say God gives the earth rational, speaking life so that it testifies for the obedient and against sinners; the Prophet is reported to have said it will tell every deed done on it.
rows.anchor: والثاني : وهو قول الجمهور : أن الله تعالى يجعل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says this testimony is possible because, in his theology, a body need not already have the usual structure to receive life; he cites ʿAli addressing the treasury as a witness to his just conduct.
rows.anchor: لأن البنية عندنا ليست شرطا لقبول الحياة

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites allow speech to be created in an inanimate object; God could create distinct sounds in the earth, with God as the speaker and witness.
rows.anchor: المعتزلة : أن الكلام يجوز خلقه في الجماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase that day is appositional to when, and both are governed by the verb tell.
rows.anchor: يومئذ بدل من إذا وناصبهما تحدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although telling usually suggests intimacy, here it pictures the earth confiding its complaints to God's friends and the angels.
rows.anchor: أن الأرض كأنها تبث شكواها إلى أولياء الله وملائكته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The causal preposition links God's inspiration to the earth's telling: it gives its news because God inspired it.
rows.anchor: ومعناه تحدث أخبارها بسبب إيحاء ربك لها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda explains inspired to it as inspired toward it and cites al-ʿAjjaj's verse as Arabic evidence for this usage.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : { أوحى لها } أي أوحى إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the earth is addressed as the beneficiary: God did this for it, so it may obtain relief from disobedient people.
rows.anchor: لعله إنما قال لها : أي فعلنا ذلك لأجلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Departure contrasts with arrival. People may leave the earth for the assembly, which fits scattered groups, or leave the assembly for reward and punishment, which fits the word depart; seeing records is more literal than seeing recompense, though both are possible.
rows.anchor: الصدور ضد الورد فالوارد الجائي والصادر والمنصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation pictures the blessed traveling with fine clothes and bright faces, announced as God's friends, while enemies go barefoot, naked, shackled, and black-faced.
rows.anchor: سود الوجوه حفاة عراة مع السلاسل والأغلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the groups as religious communities, each kind traveling with its own kind.
rows.anchor: أشتاتا أي كل فريق مع شكله اليهودي مع اليهودي والنصراني مع النصراني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation says people come from every direction and region of the earth.
rows.anchor: أشتاتا من أقطار الأرض من كل ناحية

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say people see their written records, which are placed before them and identified as their own transactions.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم : ليروا صحائف أعمالهم

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say they see the recompense of their deeds, Paradise or Fire; calling recompense a deed is apt because it corresponds to the deed itself.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : ليروا جزاء أعمالهم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet's reading has the verb with an open ya.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم : { ليروا } بالفتح

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi defines a tiny particle as the smallest ant.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي : الذرة أصغر النمل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas defines it as each grain of dust adhering to the palm after touching the ground; God shows people every small or large good and evil deed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : إذا وضعت راحتك على الأرض ثم رفعتها

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: In one transmission from ʿAsim, the ya in the verb is nominative; the remaining readers use the fatha, and some readers use jussive mood.
rows.anchor: في رواية عن عاصم : { يره } برفع الياء

rows.speaker: أحمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Al-Qurazi says an unbeliever sees the worldly reward for good deeds but receives nothing from them in the afterlife; Ibn ʿAbbas also transmits this interpretation.
rows.anchor: قال أحمد بن كعب القرظي : { فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة } من خير وهو كافر

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet tells Abu Bakr that disliked worldly experiences expiate tiny evils, while God stores tiny goods for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: ما رأيت في الدنيا مما تكره فبمثاقيل ذر الشر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says every believer and unbeliever is shown good and evil: God forgives believers' sins and rewards their good, while rejecting unbelievers' good and punishing their sins.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : ليس من مؤمن ولا كافر عمل خيرا أو شرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third answer allows deeds to be weighed even when unbelievers' good is canceled and believers' sins forgiven: their good offsets part of unbelief's punishment, and the converse applies to believers.
rows.anchor: أن حسنات الكافر وإن كانت محبطة بكفره ولكن الموازنة معتبرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth answer restricts the general promise to the blessed for tiny good and the wretched for tiny evil.
rows.anchor: المراد فمن يعمل من السعداء مثقال ذرة خيرا يره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Counting small deeds is generosity: even a small sin contains disrespect, and even a small act of obedience honors God; pure intention matters more than quantity.
rows.anchor: ثم التحقيق أن المقصود هو النية والقصد

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb reports that a person entered Paradise by lending a needle in God's cause and a woman entered it after contributing one grain to Jerusalem's construction.
rows.anchor: ما روى عن كعب : لا تحقروا شيئا من المعروف

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: When ʿAʾisha gave a petitioner one grape from a bunch, she rebuked those who laughed and recited the verse to teach that tiny deeds count.
rows.anchor: وعن عائشة : ( كانت بين يديها عنب فقدمته إلى نسوة بحضرتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An account depicts ʿAʾisha distributing 180,000 dirhams sent by Ibn al-Zubayr, then having no meat for dinner because she had forgotten to reserve money.
rows.anchor: روى : ( أن ابن الزبير بعث إليها بمائة ألف وثمانين ألف درهم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the verse was revealed about one man who minimized small alms and another who dismissed minor sins, urging small good and warning that little sins may grow.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : نزلت هذه الآية في رجلين

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet urges people to shield themselves from the Fire with even half a date, or a kind word if they have nothing else.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال عليه السلام : ( اتقوا النار ولو بشق تمرة ، فمن لم يجد فبكلمة طيبة )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies al-ʿAdiyat as a Meccan surah of eleven verses.
rows.anchor: إحدى عشرة آية مكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb baʿthara was previously explained as raising, stirring, and bringing out; another reading is baḥthara.
rows.anchor: أن معنى : { بعثرت } بعث وأثير وأخرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says what lies in graves rather than who lies there because nonresponsible contents are more numerous, or because the dead are not rational and alive until after resurrection.
rows.anchor: هو أن ما في الأرض من غير المكلفين أكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first pronoun refers to things in the graves, while the later pronoun refers to people once they have been raised alive and rational.
rows.anchor: فلا جرم كان الضمير الأول ضمير غير العقلاء ، والضمير الثاني ضمير العقلاء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda glosses the verb as distinguishing what is in the breasts.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة ، أي ميز ما في الصدور

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says a thing's yield is what remains after the rest disappears; the author cites Labid's verse as poetic evidence for the word's usage.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث : الحاصل من كل شيء ما بقي وثبت وذهب سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that the contents of hearts are gathered and displayed together in written records.
rows.anchor: معنى حصل جمع في الصحف ، أي أظهرت محصلا مجموعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation distinguishes obligatory, recommended, permissible, disliked, and forbidden acts; a sieve is called a distinguisher because it sorts things.
rows.anchor: التمييز بين الواجب ، والمندوب ، والمباح ، والمكروه ، والمحظور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation says inner secrets, often unlike outward appearances, will be exposed and veils torn away.
rows.anchor: فإنه تتكشف الأسرار وتبتهك الأستار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse admonishes people who prepare graves, coffins, and shrouds for worldly death but fail to prepare for the judgment that will uncover what lies in the earth.
rows.anchor: يقال : هذا كله للديدان ، فأين حظ الرحمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb is also read with fatha and lightening, meaning that what is in the breasts becomes manifest.
rows.anchor: وقرىء وحصل بالفتح والتخفيف بمعنى ظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's being described as fully aware on that day does not imply prior ignorance; one explanation contrasts created beings who learn by testing with God's everlasting knowledge.
rows.anchor: فإنه يصير بسبب الاختبار عالما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning that day specifies the time of recompense: no other judge can make a ruling stand or scholar make a legal answer prevail then, whereas God never forgets an answer.
rows.anchor: وقت الجزاء ، وتقريره لمن الملك كأنه يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse singles out heart-work because bodily acts follow the motives and intentions of the heart, which is the basis for blame and praise.
rows.anchor: لأن أعمال الجوارح تابعة لأعمال القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart naturally loves knowing and serving God; the resisting self is located near the chest, hence the verses speak of whispering in breasts and opening a breast to Islam.
rows.anchor: إنما المنازع في هذا الباب هو النفس ومحلسها ما يقرب من الصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural pronoun can refer to generic humanity, as in the verse saying humanity is in loss before making an exception for believers.
rows.anchor: كقوله تعالى : { إن الإنسان * لفي * خسر }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes that God knows temporal particulars, since it states that He knows people's specific conditions on that day; denying this makes one an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تعدل على كونه تعالى عالما بالجزئيات الزمانيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says al-Hajjaj accidentally used the accusative and omitted the lām from fully aware to avoid a grammatical solecism; some praise the eloquence of this response.
rows.anchor: نقل أن الحجاج سبق على لسانه أن بالنصب

rows.speaker: بعض المشايخ
rows.claim: Some scholars call the reported omission unbelief because they say it intended to alter the revealed wording.
rows.anchor: فزعم بعض المشايخ أن هذا كفر لأنه قصد لتغيير المنزل

rows.speaker: أبو السماءل
rows.claim: Abu al-Samaʾl is reported to have recited in this form.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن أبي السماءل أنه قرأ على هذا الوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next surah answers the previous surah's implied question about what that Day is: it is the Calamity.
rows.anchor: فكأنه قيل : وما ذلك اليوم ؟ فقيل هي القارعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qariʿ means a forceful, forceful blow; by extension a major disaster is called a qariʿa. The author gives related verbs and nouns for striking, blows, and knocking.
rows.anchor: القرع الضرب بشدة واعتماد ، ثم سميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All agree that the Qariʿa is a name for the Resurrection, but differ about why it bears that name.
rows.anchor: واتفقوا على أن القارعة اسم من أسماء القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is the blast that destroys creation: the first blast removes reason, the second kills all but Israfil, God then kills and revives him, and a third blast raises everyone; a report says each dead person has a designated trumpet opening.
rows.anchor: أن سبب ذلك هو الصيحة التي تموت منها الخلائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is the violent collision of celestial and earthly bodies when the world is destroyed.
rows.anchor: أن الأجرام العلوية والسفلية يصطكان اصطكاكا شديدا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the Day is named for its terrors striking people through cosmic upheaval: skies split, celestial bodies scatter, mountains are crushed, and earth is folded and changed.
rows.anchor: أن القارعة هي التي تقرع الناس بالأهوال والإفزاع

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says it strikes God's enemies with punishment, disgrace, and humiliation; a scholar prefers this over al-Kalbi because the righteous are safe from that day's terror.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مقاتل ، قال بعض المحققين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated word may function as a warning, with either nominative or accusative construction, like a repeated command to beware of a lion.
rows.anchor: أنه تحذير وقد / جاء التحذير بالرفع والنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, an implied verb says the Calamity will come as foretold by the verse about the contents of graves being brought out; or the first noun is a subject and the question is its predicate.
rows.anchor: وفيه إضمار أي ستأتيكم القارعة على ما أخبرت عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question teaches new knowledge by showing that this Calamity exceeds every ordinary calamity in terror and severity.
rows.anchor: فبهذا التجهيل علمنا أنها قارعة فاقت القوارع في الهول والشدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Calamity's nature exceeds anyone's imagination: worldly calamities and fire pale beside it, so the closing description of a scorching fire matches the surah's opening.
rows.anchor: قوارع الدنيا في جنب تلك القارعة كأنها ليست بقوارع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question marks that no one can know its full reality; the details of contingent events are known only through God's revelation, not rational demonstration.
rows.anchor: لأنها في الشدة بحيث لا يبلغها وهم أحد

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The scholars say the Qariʿa formula is rhetorically stronger than the corresponding formula for the Real Event because later warning should intensify, but the Real Event is stronger semantically as justice, while the Calamity assaults hearts with terror.
rows.anchor: قال المحققون قوله : { القارعة * ما القارعة } أشد من قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording asks what the Calamity is, but does not ask what the Abyss is, because a calamity is perceptible whereas the Abyss's nature is not.
rows.anchor: الفرق أن كونها قارعة أمر محسوس

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The temporal phrase is governed by an implied verb indicated by the Calamity: it strikes on the day when people and mountains have these conditions.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب الكشاف : الظرف نصب بمضمر دلت عليه القارعة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines moths as creatures that flutter into fire and says they are named for spreading out; people after resurrection move in panic in different directions without a clear aim.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : الفراش هو الحيوان الذي يتهافت في النار

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra compares the people to masses of locusts piling on one another; this highlights their number, whereas moths show directionless movement.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : كغوغاء الجراد يركب بعضه بعضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People at resurrection surge over one another like locusts and moths, as other verses describe their coming in crowds and surging together.
rows.anchor: لأنهم لما بعثوا يموج بعضهم في بعض كالجراد والفراش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same people can resemble moths and locusts in different respects: moths scatter in different directions, while locusts show great numbers and succession; alternatively people begin large like locusts, then become small from the sun's heat.
rows.anchor: شبه الواحد بالصغير والكبير لكن في وصفين

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet divides people into scholars, students, and a remaining rabble; the author says their later lowly state is fitting recompense.
rows.anchor: ما روى أنه عليه السلام قال : ( الناس عالم ومتعلم ، وسائر الناس همج رعاع )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that people are likened to moths because they will be more degraded than moths, which are not punished.
rows.anchor: لأنهم يكونون في ذلك اليوم أذل من الفراش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIhn is colored wool and nafsh is loosening its fibers until they spread; Ibn Masʿud reads the phrase as carded wool.
rows.anchor: والنفش فك الصوف حتى ينتفش بعضه عن بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountains have varied colors; as their structure and joined parts disperse, they resemble colored wool fluffed apart.
rows.anchor: أخبر أن الجبال مختلفة الألوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation pairs human panic with the mountains' transformation, warning Adam's children about the effect of that impact; alternatively, the mountains of Hell become red like carded wool.
rows.anchor: إنما ضم بين حال الناس وبين حال الجبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains pass through several states: crushed pieces, then heaps of sand, then fine scattered particles, and finally mirage.
rows.anchor: قد وصف الله تعالى تغير الأحوال على الجبال من وجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding the clause about the mountains with wa intensifies the warning more than simply joining the two descriptions without that repeated verb.
rows.anchor: لأن التكوير في مثل هذا المقام أبلغ في التحذير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's heat surpasses every other fire, making the word scorching an adequate warning of its intensity; the author closes with a prayer for the promised reward and protection from disgrace.
rows.anchor: أن سائر النيران بالنسبة إليها كأنها ليست حامية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says greed for wealth distracts people until death and only then do they bequeath funds for alms and pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: الحرص على المال وطلب تكثيره حتى منعتم الحقوق المالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says accumulation distracts from religion; people have hearts like stones that soften only when they visit graves, though even this slight response is inadequate.
rows.anchor: فلا تلتفتون إلى الدين ، بل قلوبكم كأنها أحجار لا تنكسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving the object of distracted unspecified makes the rebuke broader, covering neglect of remembrance, obligations, recommended acts, knowledge, worship, reflection, and contemplation.
rows.anchor: لأن المطلق أبلغ في الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read in context, accumulation distracts either from preparing for the Calamity before death or from remembering the grave until people reach it.
rows.anchor: ألهاكم التكاثر عن التدبر في أمر القارعة والاستعداد لها قبل الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first repetition refutes the belief that happiness lies in numbers and children; the forward reading promises that people will learn the truth after the sinner repents, disbeliever believes, and greedy person becomes ascetic.
rows.anchor: ليس الأمر كما يتوهممه هؤلاء من أن السعادة الحقيقية

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan warns against being impressed by surrounding crowds: a person dies, is judged, and arrives alone, so worldly accumulation will be abandoned.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول الحسن : لا يغرنك كثرة من ترى حولك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation makes the repetition emphatic: warning follows warning, like repeating an instruction not to do something.
rows.anchor: أنه للتأكيد ، وأنه وعيد بعد وعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation maps the repeated warnings to death, questioning in the grave, and resurrection, when the saved and damned are separated.
rows.anchor: أن الأول عند الموت حيث يقال له : لا بشرى والثاني في سؤال القبر

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak addresses the first warning to unbelievers and the second to believers, making the first a threat and the second a promise; he reportedly read it that way.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك سوف تعلمون ، أيها الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view says people know moral categories now but not their full consequences; experience at sight, resurrection, judgment, and entry into Paradise or Hell adds knowledge and intensifies pleasure or punishment.
rows.anchor: لكن لا يعرف قدر آثارها ونتائجها

rows.speaker: ذر
rows.claim: Dharr says he doubted punishment in the grave until he heard ʿAli use the repeated warning as evidence; the word then marks the death between two lives.
rows.anchor: كما روى عن ذر أنه قال : كنت أشك في عذاب القبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to if is omitted, not the statement that people will see Hell: a conditional answer would negate that certain vision, and a later certain question about bliss cannot sensibly follow an unreal event.
rows.anchor: اتفقوا على أن جواب لو محذوف ، وأنه ليس قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking the vision as inward perception in worldly life would avoid the contradiction but departs from the apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: ترك الظاهر خلاف الأصل

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash supplies the omitted answer: if people knew with certainty, accumulation would not distract them.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش : { لو تعلمون علم اليقين } ما ألهاكم التكاثر

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says the omitted answer means that knowledge of one's duties or purpose of creation would make one adhere to them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم لو علمتم ماذا يجب عليكم لتمسكتم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view says leaving the answer unstated lets the imagination supply an immeasurably frightening result: if they knew, they would do something beyond description, but they remain ignorant.
rows.anchor: حذف الجواب ليذهب الوهم كل مذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic lām in they will see Hell answers an unstated oath, certifying the threat; repetition with then intensifies it and magnifies terror.
rows.anchor: فاللام يدل على أنه جواب قسم محذوف

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: The repeated kalla is a rebuke, each occurrence followed by a different consequence; al-Hasan also takes it to mean truly.
rows.anchor: وكان الحسن رحمه الله يجعل معنى { كلا } في هذا الموضع بمعنى حقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Certain knowledge can mean knowledge described as certain, with the adjective placed in a genitive construction like the other cited examples.
rows.anchor: أن معناه علما يقينا فأضيف الموصوف إلى الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, certainty means death, resurrection, and the Last Day; death is called certainty because its occurrence removes doubt, so knowing its aftermath would end distraction by accumulation.
rows.anchor: أن اليقين ههنا هو الموت والبعث والقيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge strongly motivates action: before the opportunity ends it is a warning, afterward it becomes regret. The story of Dhul-Qarnayn's companions finding gems in darkness illustrates regret among both those who took few and those who took none.
rows.anchor: العلم من أشد البواعث على العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage threatens scholars: if they truly knew the harm in boasting and accumulation, they would abandon them; a scholar who does not act lacks certainty and faces woe.
rows.anchor: في الآية تهديد عظيم للعلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the open-ta reading; another reading with damma makes people be shown Hell and see it. Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisaʾi are associated with that reading, while the second verb remains open-ta.
rows.anchor: وقرىء بضمها من رأيته الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the common reading because al-Farra says it better suits Arabic as a grave threat, which should not soften the expression.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : قراءة العامة أشبه بكلام العرب

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli says the phrase means seeing Hell's punishment, since believers also see Hell when they pass over it; the author uses this to support the common reading.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي المعنى في : { لترون الجحيم } لترون عذاب الجحيم

rows.speaker: ابن عامر والكسائي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisaʾi intend the passive reading as they will be shown it, followed by seeing it themselves.
rows.anchor: وهذه القراءة تروي عن ابن عامر والكسائي كأنهما أرادا لترونها فترونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second verb in that reading shows that once they are shown Hell, they see it.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الثانية دليل على أنهم إذا أروها رأوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading repeats the second verb for emphasis and for the other rhetorical effects already discussed.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة العامة الثانية تكرير للتأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited verses show wrongdoers seeing punishment, supporting Abu ʿAli's interpretation that the threat is about witnessing Hell's torment.
rows.anchor: يدل على هذا قوله : { إذ يرون العذاب } وقوله : { وإذا رأى الذين ظلموا العذاب }
